mappings.note: Provinces under an emperor with land grants letting local chiefs govern and collect taxes is the balance of central and local power. Squarely the administrative-measures outcome.
The reach of Gupta trade in textiles, spices, ivory and gems. Economic history; no LO in this frame covers commerce.
Vaishnava rulers funding Nalanda and other monasteries is a deliberate policy towards religious institutions. Not LO-127, which would need a new movement's emergence analysed.
Why the period earns the 'classical age' label, across literature, science, art and philosophy. Period characterisation under the goal.
Summarises Aryabhata's astronomical results. Scientific history; no LO covers science.
The span of the Brihat Samhita from astronomy to gemology. Intellectual history under the goal.
The plot of Meghadutam. Literary history; LO-128 concerns bhakti and sufi poetry and the social order, which this is not.
Ayurveda's holistic focus as set out in the Charaka Samhita. Medical and textual history.
Names Sarnath and Ajanta as centres of Gupta art. Art geography; the item asks where, not how anything was built, so not LO-126.
The balance, idealisation and serenity of Gupta sculpture. Sculptural aesthetics rather than the construction of temples, so the goal rather than LO-126.
Shows the Guptas building on Mauryan administrative models, Kushana art and older scientific work. A cross-period judgement, exactly what the goal describes.
Tests whether a love poem can serve as evidence for landscape, rivers, cities and weather. Source criticism applied to literature, so the goal.
Compares inscriptions, coins, literature and foreign accounts and what each uniquely yields. The most explicit 'types of sources' item in the chapter.
Distance, resistant local rulers, military cost and succession disputes as the standing difficulties of holding a large empire. Reasoning about control, so LO-124.

A copper-plate grant with boundaries and witnesses illustrates the Gupta practice of tax-free grants and permanent record-keeping, and part (iii) asks what it shows about the state's dealings with religious figures. Administration throughout.
Terrain on the route to a western port, evidence for Indo-Roman trade and the risks of long-distance commerce. Economic history and source inference, so the goal.

Parts (i) and (iii) are about fields of achievement and the classical-age label (CG-SST2), while part (ii) asks what supporting both court poets and Buddhist monasteries says about the emperor's policy (LO-124).

Part (i) turns on a king commissioning a large stone Shiva temple, which is the temple-building outcome, and part (iii) asks the learner to compare his actions with those of the Gupta rulers, which is the comparison outcome.
Huna raids straining the frontier while tributary rulers hold back, and how the two together unravel the empire. Reasoning about military and administrative control, so LO-124.
